0.text:
The members of Subsystem #0 are the core of **requests’ HTTP transport layer**.  
It contains the `HTTPAdapter` class (and its helper functions), the `PreparedRequest` model that turns a user-supplied request into a fully-specified HTTP message, a mix-in (`SessionRedirectMixin`) that implements redirect handling, and a collection of utility functions for proxy handling, URL quoting, and validation. Together they prepare a request, select or build a connection pool (including SOCKS/HTTPS proxies), send the request through urllib3, and process the response – raising the various exception types defined here when something goes wrong.

Because all of these pieces share the same data structures (`PreparedRequest`, `Response`, proxy settings) and are invoked by the high-level `Session` object, they are clustered together as a cohesive unit that implements **request preparation, adapter selection, connection management, and redirect logic** – the essential plumbing that turns a high-level API call into an actual HTTP transaction.

1.text: The members of this cluster implement a high-level HTTP client library. All of the functions named after HTTP verbs (`get`, `post`, `put`, …) delegate to a central **Session** class, which holds configuration (cookies, proxies, SSL settings, adapters, hooks) and provides methods such as `prepare_request`, `send`, and `merge_environment_settings` that construct a **PreparedRequest**, resolve proxies, and hand the request off to an **HTTPAdapter** for transport. Utility helpers in `utils.py` parse and validate HTTP header strings, while `exceptions.py` defines error types used throughout the flow. Because these pieces share the same data structures (Session, Request, PreparedRequest) and cooperate to turn a user-level call into a network I/O operation, they form a cohesive subsystem that encapsulates the entire request-building, sending, and response-handling pipeline of the library.

2.text: The members of this cluster form the core implementation of an HTTP **Response** object and the supporting error/utility code that lets callers read, decode, and manage the data returned from a request. All of the methods (`__iter__`, `iter_content`, `iter_lines`, `json`, `text`, `raise_for_status`, etc.) and the serialization helpers (`__getstate__`, `__setstate__`) operate on the same internal state (status code, headers, raw body) and expose a uniform, context-manager-compatible interface, while the `StreamConsumedError` exception and the utility functions (`stream_decode_response_unicode`, `iter_slices`) provide the low-level mechanics for safely streaming and chunk-splitting the raw payload. Because these pieces are tightly coupled—each method relies on the same response metadata and on the same streaming helpers—the cluster is a cohesive subsystem that isolates all response-handling logic from the rest of the library (e.g., the `HTTPAdapter.build_response` that constructs a `Response` instance). The subsystem’s purpose is therefore to encapsulate the representation of an HTTP response and to offer safe, incremental access to its content.

3.text: The subsystem is the implementation of a **cookie jar** used by the HTTP client library. All 27 members live in `src/requests/cookies.py` and together provide a dictionary-like container (`RequestsCookieJar`) that can store, retrieve, iterate, and serialize HTTP cookies, handling domain- and path-scoped naming collisions (e.g., `set` removes a cookie when the value is None, uses `remove_cookie_by_name`, and distinguishes `Morsel` objects). The supporting class `CookieConflictError` and the many helper methods (`_find`, `list_domains`, `get_dict`, pickling hooks, etc.) give the jar the logic needed to locate cookies without duplicates, enforce a policy, and expose a familiar mapping API to callers such as `Session.prepare_request` and `cookiejar_from_dict`. Thus the module is a cohesive unit because it encapsulates all state-management and lookup behavior for HTTP cookies, keeping that concern separate from request preparation, connection handling, or higher-level session logic.

4.text:
The fourth subsystem groups together the data-type helpers and the exception hierarchy that the **requests** package uses to model HTTP operations.  
The classes in `src/requests/_types.py` (e.g., `SupportsRead`, `SupportsItems`, `_ValidatedRequest`, `BaseRequestKwargs` and its concrete subclasses) define protocols and lightweight containers for the arguments that can be passed to the various HTTP verbs (`GET`, `POST`, etc.). The classes in `src/requests/exceptions.py` (`RequestException` and its many subclasses such as `ConnectionError`, `Timeout`, `SSLError`, etc.) provide a structured set of error types that can be raised by the transport layer and later inspected by callers.  

Both groups are tightly coupled: the request-argument types are validated and stored, and when something goes wrong the code raises one of the defined exception classes, often attaching the original `request` and `response` objects (as shown in `RequestException.__init__`). Keeping these definitions together makes the public API consistent, lets the rest of the library raise and catch a predictable set of errors, and centralises the typing/validation logic for request parameters.

5.text: The subsystem implements lightweight dictionary-like containers that treat string keys without regard to case. `CaseInsensitiveDict` stores a normal mapping internally but normalises look-ups (and deletions, containment checks, etc.) by lower-casing the key, while preserving the original capitalisation for iteration and representation; it also supplies helpers such as `lower_items` and a `copy` method. `LookupDict` is a thin wrapper that forwards attribute access and item access to an underlying mapping, providing a convenient “dot-lookup” style API. Both classes are used throughout the HTTP client (e.g., when building request/response headers, initializing sessions, and constructing adapters) to handle HTTP header dictionaries, which must be case-insensitive according to the HTTP spec. The module groups these structures together because they share the same purpose—providing consistent, case-insensitive, mutable mappings for header-related data—so that the rest of the code can rely on a single, well-encapsulated implementation.

6.text: The six-member subsystem implements a lightweight “request-like” object that mimics the interface expected by the `http.cookiejar` machinery in the Python standard library. All of the methods (`get_type`, `get_host`, `get_full_url`, `has_header`, `add_header`, etc.) simply forward information from an underlying `requests.Response` (`self._r`) and expose it through the same attribute names (`origin_req_host`, `unverifiable`, etc.) that `http.cookiejar` calls when extracting or sending cookies. Because `extract_cookies_to_jar` and `get_cookie_header` are the only external callers, the class exists as a cohesive adapter layer that lets the rest of the code reuse the existing `requests` objects while satisfying the cookie-jar API without pulling in the full `urllib.request` request objects. The implementation is purely structural – it parses URLs, rebuilds them with a custom Host header, and stores any new headers, but it does not contain any business-logic beyond adapting the request representation.

7.text: The members of Subsystem #7 are all the code that implements the **HTTP Digest authentication handler** used by the `requests` library. All of the classes, methods and helper functions (`build_digest_header`, the various hash-algorithm helpers, `handle_401`, `handle_redirect`, `__call__`, etc.) work together to parse a server’s `WWW-Authenticate: Digest …` challenge, compute the appropriate response hash (MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-512, etc.), and attach the resulting `Authorization` header to outgoing requests, while also managing per-thread state and cookie handling. Because these responsibilities are tightly coupled—parsing the challenge, selecting the algorithm, generating the nonce count, and formatting the header—they are grouped into a single cohesive unit (the `HTTPDigestAuth` class) that can be passed around as a plug-in authentication object for any request. The subsystem does not appear to be used elsewhere in the call-graph, which is typical for an optional authentication mechanism that is only invoked when a request requires Digest auth.

8.text: The members of Subsystem #8 are all defined in `src/requests/cookies.py` (and a few helpers in `src/requests/utils.py`) and they revolve around constructing, converting, and manipulating cookie objects and cookie jars. Functions such as **`create_cookie`**, **`morsel_to_cookie`**, **`extract_cookies_to_jar`**, **`merge_cookies`**, **`cookiejar_from_dict`**, and **`add_dict_to_cookiejar`** build `Cookie` instances, translate between Python’s `http.cookies.Morsel` and the `RequestsCookieJar` type, and combine or serialize cookie collections; the `MockResponse` class provides a minimal response-like object that supplies header information needed by those utilities. Because many higher-level components (e.g., `Session`, `PreparedRequest`, `HTTPAdapter`, authentication handlers) need a reliable way to read, write, and merge HTTP cookies across requests, this set of functions and the mock response class are grouped together as a self-contained cookie-handling subsystem. The code does not reveal any business-specific logic—its purpose is purely to manage HTTP cookie data in a consistent format for the rest of the Requests library.

9.text: The nine components form the request-handling core of the library: a **BaseAdapter** abstraction that knows how to **send** a request and **close** the underlying transport, and a **Request** model that can be **prepared** into a **PreparedRequest**. The mix-in **RequestHooksMixin** supplies a dictionary-based hook registry (events → callables) together with methods to **register**, **deregister** and validate hooks, which the Request object inherits so that user-supplied callbacks can be attached to lifecycle events (e.g., “response”, “pre-request”). All of the members share the same responsibility of turning a high-level request description into a low-level, transport-ready object while allowing extensible processing via hooks, which is why they are clustered together as a cohesive subsystem. The exact business purpose (e.g., HTTP client vs. generic RPC) cannot be inferred beyond the fact that it provides an adapter-based, hook-enabled request pipeline.

10.text: The ten-member subsystem groups together utilities that turn user-supplied request data into the low-level byte payloads required by HTTP. `RequestEncodingMixin` (and its methods `path_url`, `_encode_params`, `_encode_files`) implements the logic for building query strings, encoding form fields, and constructing multipart/form-data bodies, while helper functions such as `has_read`, `merge_setting`, `guess_filename`, `from_key_val_list`, and `to_key_val_list` provide small, reusable pieces for type-checking, merging configuration, extracting filenames, and converting between dictionary and list representations of parameters. These functions are called by higher-level request-preparation code (`PreparedRequest.prepare_body`, `Session.prepare_request`, etc.), so the subsystem forms a cohesive unit that isolates all encoding-related concerns (parameter serialization, file handling, and related settings) from the rest of the HTTP client. The repeated references to `OrderedDict`, `RequestField`, and `encode_multipart_formdata` indicate that the module’s purpose is strictly to produce correctly formatted request bodies, not to perform any network I/O.

11.text: The eleven objects in this cluster implement the authentication plug-in used by the **requests** HTTP client. `AuthBase` defines the callable interface that a request-auth object must provide, and the concrete subclasses `HTTPBasicAuth` and `HTTPProxyAuth` supply the logic for standard Basic authentication (for origin servers and for HTTP proxies respectively). Each subclass stores a username and password, implements `__call__` so that a `PreparedRequest` can attach the appropriate `Authorization` or `Proxy-Authorization` header (via the helper `_basic_auth_str`), and defines equality/inequality helpers (`__eq__`, `__ne__`) that compare the stored credentials using `getattr` and `all`. The subsystem is kept together because all of these classes share the same contract (`AuthBase.__call__`) and are invoked uniformly by `PreparedRequest.prepare_auth`, allowing the rest of the library to treat any authentication mechanism as a single interchangeable component.
